title: Advanced Joins, Self-Joins & CROSS JOINs Narration Scripts

lecture.New_Day11Part1audio01.mp3: Welcome to Day 11! Today, we ascend into advanced relational operations: Self-Joins, Cross-Joins, and Non-Equi Joins. These techniques enable you to unravel organizational hierarchies, generate analytical Cartesian matrices, and compare rows against other rows in the same table.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio02.mp3: A Self-Join occurs when a table is joined to itself. In database architecture, entities often possess recursive relationships: an employee has a manager who is also an employee, or a category has a parent category that lives in the same table.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio03.mp3: To execute a Self-Join, you must assign distinct aliases to the two instances of the same table, treating them as if they were completely different entities in memory.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio04.mp3: In Query 1, we join employees aliased as emp with employees aliased as mgr, matching emp dot manager ID to mgr dot employee ID. This produces the employee's name alongside their direct manager's name.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio05.mp3: Using a LEFT JOIN in a self-join is essential when top-level leaders or root nodes exist. If you use an INNER JOIN, the CEO or top director with a NULL manager ID will be silently dropped from your results!
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio06.mp3: In Query 2, we use a self-join with aggregation to calculate the management span of control, counting how many direct reports each manager oversees.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio07.mp3: Self-joins also power peer comparisons. By joining on the same department ID and using an inequality on employee ID, you can pair colleagues without duplicate or mirror pairs.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio08.mp3: In Query 3, we pair employees within the same department to inspect peer staffing distributions.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio09.mp3: Now, let's explore the CROSS JOIN. A CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product of two tables: every single row from Table A is paired with every single row from Table B.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio10.mp3: If Table A contains 10 rows and Table B contains 5 rows, a CROSS JOIN generates exactly 50 rows. Because row counts multiply exponentially, always ensure your input datasets are deliberately sized.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio11.mp3: In Query 4, we cross-join departments with customer regions to generate a complete business coverage matrix for marketing expansion.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio12.mp3: CROSS JOINs are also indispensable when computing percentage contributions. By cross-joining a table with a scalar summary subquery, you can calculate each row's share of total company volume.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio13.mp3: Non-Equi Joins use comparison operators other than equals, such as greater than, less than, or BETWEEN. These are common in price tiering, commission lookups, and overlapping date intervals.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio14.mp3: In Query 5, we use a Non-Equi Join to compare product prices against higher-priced items within the same product category.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio15.mp3: Database performance tip: Self-joins on large tables require indexed foreign keys. Ensure columns like manager ID and parent ID have dedicated B-Tree indexes.
lecture.New_Day11Part1audio16.mp3: You're now equipped with advanced joining techniques! Let's step into the practice lab and solve hierarchical and matrix analytics challenges.

questions.New_Day11Question01.mp3: Map employee-to-manager hierarchy! Perform a LEFT JOIN on employees to itself, returning employee ID, employee first name, job title, and manager name using COALESCE to display Top Executive for leaders with no manager.
questions.New_Day11Question01sol.mp3: Let's perform a self-join. SELECT emp.employee_id, emp.first_name AS employee_name, emp.job_title, COALESCE of mgr.first_name || ' ' || mgr.last_name, 'Top Executive' AS manager_name... FROM employees emp LEFT JOIN employees mgr ON emp.manager_id = mgr.employee_id.
questions.New_Day11Question02.mp3: Calculate management span of control! Join managers to employees on manager ID, returning manager first name, manager last name, and total direct reports, ordered by direct reports descending.
questions.New_Day11Question02sol.mp3: Let's count direct reports. SELECT mgr.first_name AS manager_first_name, mgr.last_name AS manager_last_name, COUNT of emp.employee_id AS direct_reports... FROM employees mgr INNER JOIN employees emp ON mgr.employee_id = emp.manager_id... GROUP BY mgr.employee_id, mgr.first_name, mgr.last_name... ORDER BY direct_reports DESC.
questions.New_Day11Question03.mp3: Find high-earning subordinates! Self-join employees to find staff earning at least 70 percent of their manager's salary. Return employee name, employee salary, manager name, and manager salary.
questions.New_Day11Question03sol.mp3: Let's compare subordinate and manager salaries. SELECT emp.first_name AS employee_name, emp.salary AS employee_salary, mgr.first_name AS manager_name, mgr.salary AS manager_salary... FROM employees emp INNER JOIN employees mgr ON emp.manager_id = mgr.employee_id... WHERE emp.salary >= mgr.salary * 0.70... ORDER BY emp.salary DESC.
questions.New_Day11Question04.mp3: Same-department peer pairs! Self-join employees to generate unique pairs of colleagues who work in the same department, using an inequality to prevent self-pairing and mirror duplicates.
questions.New_Day11Question04sol.mp3: Let's match department peers. SELECT e1.first_name AS emp1_name, e2.first_name AS emp2_name, e1.department_id... FROM employees e1 INNER JOIN employees e2 ON e1.department_id = e2.department_id AND e1.employee_id < e2.employee_id... ORDER BY e1.department_id, e1.first_name.
questions.New_Day11Question05.mp3: Category hierarchy traversal! Self-join categories to return subcategory name and its corresponding parent category name where parent ID is not null.
questions.New_Day11Question05sol.mp3: Let's link subcategories to parents. SELECT sub.name AS subcategory_name, parent.name AS parent_category_name... FROM categories sub INNER JOIN categories parent ON sub.parent_id = parent.id.
questions.New_Day11Question06.mp3: Identify root categories! Query categories to return category ID and category name for all top-level categories that have no parent category.
questions.New_Day11Question06sol.mp3: Let's find root categories. SELECT id AS category_id, name AS category_name... FROM categories... WHERE parent_id IS NULL.
questions.New_Day11Question07.mp3: Generate department-region coverage matrix! Perform a CROSS JOIN between departments and distinct customer regions. Return department name and region.
questions.New_Day11Question07sol.mp3: Let's create a Cartesian coverage matrix. SELECT d.department_name, r.region... FROM departments d CROSS JOIN subquery of distinct region from customers r... ORDER BY d.department_name, r.region.
questions.New_Day11Question08.mp3: Simulate product fulfillment scenarios! CROSS JOIN the first 3 products with all distinct order statuses. Return product name and status.
questions.New_Day11Question08sol.mp3: Let's generate product status scenarios. SELECT p.name AS product_name, s.status... FROM subquery of products limit 3 p CROSS JOIN subquery of distinct status from orders s... ORDER BY p.name, s.status.
questions.New_Day11Question09.mp3: Find higher-priced category peers! For product ID 101, perform a non-equi self-join on products in the same category to find peers with a strictly higher unit price.
questions.New_Day11Question09sol.mp3: Let's find more expensive peers. SELECT p1.name AS product_name, p1.unit_price, p2.name AS higher_priced_product, p2.unit_price AS higher_price... FROM products p1 INNER JOIN products p2 ON p1.category_id = p2.category_id AND p2.unit_price > p1.unit_price... WHERE p1.product_id = 101.
questions.New_Day11Question10.mp3: Regional customer co-location pairs! Self-join customers to find pairs of distinct customers located within the same geographic region, avoiding reverse duplicates.
questions.New_Day11Question10sol.mp3: Let's pair co-located customers. SELECT c1.first_name AS customer1, c2.first_name AS customer2, c1.region... FROM customers c1 INNER JOIN customers c2 ON c1.region = c2.region AND c1.customer_id < c2.customer_id... ORDER BY c1.region, c1.first_name.
questions.New_Day11Question11.mp3: Departmental hierarchy rollup! Join employees to their manager via self-join, and join with departments. Return employee name, job title, manager name, and department name.
questions.New_Day11Question11sol.mp3: Let's chain self-join with departments. SELECT emp.first_name AS employee_name, emp.job_title, COALESCE of mgr.first_name, 'None' AS manager_name, d.department_name... FROM employees emp LEFT JOIN employees mgr ON emp.manager_id = mgr.employee_id INNER JOIN departments d ON emp.department_id = d.department_id.
questions.New_Day11Question12.mp3: Detect company executives! From employees, return employee ID, first name, last name, job title, and salary for staff who have no manager assigned.
questions.New_Day11Question12sol.mp3: Let's identify executives without managers. SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, job_title, salary... FROM employees... WHERE manager_id IS NULL.
questions.New_Day11Question13.mp3: Multi-condition order filtering! Join orders with customers on customer ID, filtering for North region customers with total amount 10000 or greater.
questions.New_Day11Question13sol.mp3: Let's filter on joined conditions. SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date, o.total_amount, c.first_name AS customer_name, c.region... FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND c.region = 'North' AND o.total_amount >= 10000.
questions.New_Day11Question14.mp3: Inventory share percentage! Cross-join products with a subquery of total inventory stock, calculating each product's stock percentage rounded to 2 decimals.
questions.New_Day11Question14sol.mp3: Let's calculate inventory share. SELECT p.product_id, p.name, p.stock_qty, ROUND of p.stock_qty times 100.0 divided by total.sum_stock, 2 AS stock_pct... FROM products p CROSS JOIN subquery of SUM of stock_qty from products total... ORDER BY stock_pct DESC.
questions.New_Day11Question15.mp3: Executive reporting view! Return employee name, salary, manager name, and department name, ordered from highest salary to lowest.
questions.New_Day11Question15sol.mp3: Let's build an executive hierarchy view. SELECT emp.first_name AS employee_name, emp.salary, mgr.first_name AS manager_name, d.department_name... FROM employees emp LEFT JOIN employees mgr ON emp.manager_id = mgr.employee_id LEFT JOIN departments d ON emp.department_id = d.department_id... ORDER BY emp.salary DESC.
